doc.title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

title: Grandmother Suzanne LeBlanc, nurse on a plantation
summary: Edna describes her grandmother Suzanne LeBlanc, a French-speaking nurse who cared for a white planter's family and was given a plantation house.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And, um, I want to say this. My, my famous grandmother, who I take after, was Suzanne. That's French. S-A-Z, how do you spell Suzanne? S-A-S-U-Z-A-N-E. S-U-Z-A-N-E.

Suzanne. She doesn't like Susan. But her name was Suzanne LeBlanc. And she was a grand old lady of the whole family. She had this big plantation home that her husband died in her four-post bed. And he was a white man. He was a pure white man. You want me to tell? Sure. You want me to tell her why? She was a nurse. And so she took care of his face with, um, I think he had four boys. One just recently died out there in, uh, Ascension Parish. I'm sorry I didn't get to see him. Because he asked for me. One, not me, he didn't know me. But he asked of one of Johnny Beboleyn's children. And, uh, so I was the only one left. And my uncle out there, he said, why didn't I go to see him? Because he was a very rich man. Perhaps he would have gave me something. So, uh, this man was, um, what's my grandfather's name? Uh, Bebole?
The old man, my sister took the old man's picture. Oh yeah, LeBlanc. Huh? Huh?
No, Johnny Bebole was my, my father. But, uh, the old man LeBlanc that died in my grand, my grandmother's bed. Oh yeah. Uh, hmm.

Those old people, they come and they go. The names come and go. But anyway, he was an old Frenchman. And my grandmother was a nurse. She spoke French. His wife had cancer. And he called her in to take care of his wife and his children. We had four children. And she died. My grandmother still stayed there and took care of the children, boys, the four daughters. They adored my grandmother. They did everything for her. Everything. One of them was a lawyer. The other two were something. But anyway, they took care of her until she died. And so, they had this beautiful plantation. Not the, not the house that he lived in. But this house that he gave my grandmother is out there now. We go, I take my children out there to see it all the time. They're still standing. And, um, I showed them the room that my grandmother lived in. And then, my mother and my grandfather died in. And, you know, it's very big four-poster bed. Have you ever seen them? Yeah. Hi, hi, baby. You can step up on a step to get in. Well, that's the bed like that he died in. And so, he left word when he died to his son to always take care of her because she was so good to their mother. And until they died, they took care of her. She was such a sweet old lady. All the people in the countryside in those days, they didn't have no automobiles at all. They had these, uh, carriages. Now, you see these carriages that we rode in the other day? That wasn't new to me. I rode in those that go to school. To go to school. Because we went to school, uh, we live in a mile and a half from Donaldsonville. In this great big plantation home. We had the largest home out there. And if you have a chance to make a trip out there, I can tell you where this home is and you can see it. It's well kept, beautiful, and the people will let you go in there. If you just say the Bibeles, uh, uh, wants to someone from the Bibeles family want to see the home. So, uh, it's really, and it's well kept up until this very day. While all the other places are gone, that's still standing. So, uh, um, my mother, after my grandmother died in that home, my mother lived there. She raised her family there with my father. My father died first. My father died there in that home. And then we came to New Orleans because my mother was a dressmaker from Odise. And she sold for the Bartons. You know of the Bartons? They're very, very rich plantation homes out there in Ascension or Assumption Parish. Their home is out there. On that road, on that new road. The Bartons, they, they're, oh, well known. Oh, it should be in history.
